chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
title: The Jersey cow in the graveyard and Earl Hines's funeral-home story
summary: Taking a shortcut by the graveyard at night, he nearly died of fright meeting a Jersey cow; Stanley answers with Earl Hines's funeral-home story.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: No wonder you didn't want to do any extra walking.

Yes. And we had plenty of walking to do. And a lot of times, you know, see, it's dark. A lot of times, I'd figure, well, I'll take a shortcut through the -- by the graveyard, you know. But when you take the shortcut through the graveyard, you're on one little path, see? You know, just a path, just -- you've seen a country path. And I'd
be walking along, whistling, (whistles) looking around, looking around --
(Laughter.)

And so one night, I came through there and you see, it was a Jersey cow was across the path. Well, a Jersey cow is brown, but there's always a white spot that shows. And when I walked up on this Jersey cow, I couldn't see anything but that white spot doing this.
(Laughter.)
Oh, that was the worst feeling. It was. And then lucky, the cow said, 'Moo.' Oh, I felt so -- I felt relieved when the cow said, 'Moo.' Oh, boy, I'll tell you.

That's like Earl's story when he went in the funeral home, when he was in Pittsburgh and one of his kid friends -- his father ran this place, you know, and the father had got the corpse ready, but he'd gone in the back to get some cufflinks and Earl and his friend were standing there and the corpse slipped or something and went -- 'ugh'
(Laughter.)

-- and poor Earl ran out of there so fast, he knocked the casket over and the man came to see his father about it, because he'd damaged his casket, and when he found out why Earl went out, he said, (inaudible).
(Laughter.)
Oh, those things can happen.
Yeah, well, he wouldn't have been
very old then.
How's that?
How old would you have been when that happened?
I was about 12, 13. 12 or 13 years old.
That was a lot of walking and those buckets got heavy.

Yes, they got heavy. They really got heavy. And the thing about it, you know, everybody had a job, you know, and that was my job to do that. So he told me, "I don't care what you do. If you don't get home until 11:00 at night, you got to go over and do that." So consequently, it taught me responsibility, but I didn't like any parts of it.
(Laughter.)
